> **What this case shows** — gait is measured in many modalities (angles, forces,
> muscle activity, IMU); the integrative question is *what they share*. Fusing real
> **kinematics** (joint angles) and **kinetics** (ground reaction force) of 42
> adults across 8 speeds, the ecosystem finds a coupling a single number would
> miss: **CCA** gives a top canonical correlation of **0.87** between the
> modalities, and **JIVE**'s cross-modal **joint** component tracks walking speed
> (**r = −0.70**) — the shared, speed-driven gait pattern — while most of each
> modality's variance (kinematics 79%, kinetics 62%) is modality-specific. The
> whole-block **RV is only 0.088**, which is *exactly why* you reach for CCA and
> JIVE, not RV alone. **How to read it** — left, JIVE's joint/individual/residual
> split per modality; centre, the shared component falling with speed; right, the
> tight canonical coupling.

::: {.callout-tip title="The recipe you'll learn"}
**Workflow** — to integrate two (or more) aligned modality blocks: **JIVE**
splits them into structure *shared across* modalities vs *specific to* each;
**CCA** finds the directions that co-vary most; **RV** scores the whole-block
association.
**Way of thinking** — "how related are these modalities?" has several answers:
RV asks about the *whole configuration*, CCA about the *best direction*, JIVE
about a *shared low-rank component*. A low RV with a high CCA and a meaningful JIVE
joint means the coupling is real but *low-dimensional* — read all three.
**Ecosystem usage** — `jive()`, `cca()`, `rvCoefficient()` (PhysioCrossModal) on a
list of blocks that share the observation dimension; extend with `coupledNMF()`,
`multipleFactorAnalysis()`, `multimodalGaitIndex()`.
:::

## Proposition

On real gait, integrating kinematics and kinetics recovers a strong, speed-driven
shared structure: CCA top canonical correlation 0.87, JIVE joint component vs speed
r = −0.70, with most variance modality-specific (RV only 0.088) — so CCA and JIVE,
not RV alone, reveal the coupling.

## Question & goal

**The question is integrative.** Each modality of gait tells part of the story;
the clinically and scientifically interesting part is what they hold *in common*
versus what is unique to each. The WBDS dataset provides both kinematics and
kinetics for the same trials, so we can ask directly: what do the joint angles and
the ground reaction force *share*, and does that shared part mean something (like
walking speed)?

## Challenge & approach

We build two aligned blocks — **kinematics** (right hip/knee/ankle sagittal angle
over the gait cycle) and **kinetics** (vertical GRF, time-normalised heel-strike to
heel-strike) — for 42 adults × 8 speeds. We apply **JIVE** (joint vs individual vs
residual per modality), **CCA** (canonical coupling), and **RV** (whole-block
association), and ask whether the shared component tracks speed.

## Data

**WBDS** (Fukuchi et al. 2018) — 42 adults, kinematics + kinetics across 8 treadmill
speeds. Details in [`artifacts/data_sources.json`](artifacts/data_sources.json).

## Results

![JIVE joint/individual/residual variance per modality (left), the JIVE joint
(shared) component versus speed (centre), and the canonical coupling of kinematics
and kinetics (right).](artifacts/figure.png)

*How to read this:* the left bars show a real shared (joint) component in *both*
modalities (kinematics 21%, kinetics 38%) with larger modality-specific parts. The
centre panel shows that shared component is speed-driven (r = −0.70). The right
panel is the CCA: one direction of kinematics and one of kinetics move together at
r = 0.87.

| quantity | value |
|---|---|
| CCA top canonical correlation | **0.87** |
| JIVE joint component vs speed | **r = −0.70** |
| JIVE joint variance (kinematics / kinetics) | 0.21 / 0.38 |
| RV coefficient (whole-block) | **0.088** (p = 0.0005) |
| observations fused | 328 (42 × 8) |

## Conclusion

The modalities of gait share a real, low-dimensional, speed-driven structure that
CCA and JIVE expose — and that the whole-block RV, on its own, would hide. The
transferable takeaway: **integrate modalities with more than one lens — JIVE for
shared-vs-specific, CCA for the covarying directions, RV for the whole — because a
low RV can still hide a strong, meaningful coupling.**

## Open questions

- Adding **EMG and IMU** blocks (a genuine four-modality fusion) with
  `coupledNMF()` and a `multimodalGaitIndex()` would build a full multi-modal gait
  signature; that needs a synchronised EMG + kinematics + kinetics + IMU cohort.
  *Documented, not escalated.*

## Using this in your own analysis

| step | function | package |
|---|---|---|
| align modalities to a shared observation dimension | `alignSignals()` / `MultiPhysioExperiment()` | PhysioCrossModal |
| shared vs modality-specific structure | `jive()` | PhysioCrossModal |
| canonical coupling directions | `cca()` / `plsBlocks()` | PhysioCrossModal |
| whole-block association | `rvCoefficient()` / `distanceCorrelation()` | PhysioCrossModal |
| composite multi-modal deviation index | `multimodalGaitIndex()` | PhysioCrossModal |

**Choosing the parameters:** give a list of blocks that share rows (here
subject-speeds), pick JIVE ranks from a scree/permutation check, and read the joint
scores as the integrated representation — then relate them to an outcome (here,
speed).

```r
library(PhysioCrossModal)
fit <- jive(list(kinematics = KIN, kinetics = KINET), rank_joint = 2, rank_individual = 2)
fit$variance                       # joint / individual / residual per modality
cor(fit$joint_scores[, 1], speed)  # the shared component's meaning
cca(KIN, KINET)$cor                # canonical coupling
```
